items.lede: Today, Omnis Pleasants filed two retention applications — Dkts. 247 and 248 — both entered September 4, with a supporting exhibit package at Dkt. 246.
items.body_md:
Today, Omnis Pleasants filed two retention applications — Dkts. 247 and 248 — both entered September 4, with a supporting exhibit package at Dkt. 246. The docket descriptions identify both as "Employ (Application)" without naming the proposed professionals; the underlying documents have not been pulled as primary text. Given the procedural posture — the September 3 hearing was the contested session on, among other things, the HSF Kramer and AP Services retention applications — the most natural read is that these are either amended or supplemental applications responding to objections aired at that hearing, or new professional retentions being added to the estate's roster. Either way, they are substantive filings: retention applications contested on grounds touching estate value and conduct are not routine, and the U.S. Trustee's standing objection to HSF Kramer's disclosures remains on the record. Classification up is warranted until the underlying text confirms otherwise.

The September 3 hearing itself proceeded as scheduled — Dkt. 245 records the in-person/Zoom sign-in sheet and Dkt. 244 the 5 hour, 49 minute audio recording — but no resulting orders on cash collateral, bidding procedures, or any retention have yet appeared on the docket as of today's filing date. 
Judge Owens grilled conflicts counsel during the hearing about whether HSF Kramer should be disqualified over its prepetition work for the two lenders,
 and the absence of a ruling on the docket as of today suggests the court took the matters under advisement or directed further submissions rather than ruling from the bench. That reading is consistent with the Lowenstein Sandler scheduling letter (Dkt. 235), which proposed a separate litigation schedule for the dismissal motion (Dkt. 93) — a track Judge Owens has not yet calendared beyond the approximate November 3 hearing date. Dkts. 239–243 — the four Lowenstein Sandler and Sidley Austin PHV orders and a certificate of service on Dkt. 173 — are procedural and carry no independent weight on recovery.

Until orders issue on cash collateral and bidding procedures, the debtor continues operating under the interim cash-collateral authority granted at Dkt. 50, which 
permits use of prepetition collateral under an approved budget and grants TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC adequate protection, requires the debtor to continue the sale process, and limits any plan absent the secured parties' consent to one that pays their obligations in full in cash.
 Every day that passes without a final cash-collateral order leaves that constraint in place while the HSF Kramer disqualification question — which, if resolved against the debtor, would require replacement of lead bankruptcy counsel mid-case — remains unresolved. The next concrete milestone is entry of Judge Owens's rulings on the September 3 matters; given the complexity of the HSF Kramer record and the multiple objections to bidding procedures, written orders could arrive in days or be preceded by a supplemental hearing. The dismissal motion hearing is currently scheduled for November 3.

items.lede: On September 4, Skillz Platform Inc. filed a sealed letter with the court (Dkt. 93, Neiburg), accompanied by a second letter filed the same day that has not yet received a docket number.
items.body_md:
On September 4, Skillz Platform Inc. filed a sealed letter with the court (Dkt. 93, Neiburg), accompanied by a second letter filed the same day that has not yet received a docket number.

Both filings land the day the compel order (Dkt. 92) ripens as the controlling instrument in this proceeding, and their timing is not incidental. Sealed letters to a bankruptcy judge in an actively contested Chapter 15, submitted by the creditor that just prevailed on a motion to compel, typically serve one of a narrow set of purposes: reporting a compliance dispute with the court-ordered production and deposition deadlines; raising a privilege or confidentiality issue that has emerged from the newly compelled discovery; or surfacing a related development — in Tel Aviv or on the Second Circuit appeal docket — that Skillz wants the court to have before any scheduling ruling. The content is not on the public record, and no secondary reporting has confirmed what the letters address; any characterization beyond their timing and authorship would be speculation. What can be said with precision: Skillz chose to go to Judge Walrath directly and under seal within 48 hours of the compel order's entry, which signals either an urgent compliance issue or a sensitive factual matter that Skillz did not want to brief in the ordinary course on the public docket. The companion unnumbered letter — filed the same day without an assigned docket number as of this writing — may be a chambers copy, a cover transmission, or a separate communication from another party; the docket entry does not identify the filer, and that ambiguity should be tracked when the entry is numbered and the filer is identified.

For recovery posture, the immediate question is whether Dkt. 93 reflects a dispute over Papaya's compliance with Dkt. 92's production and deposition directives. If Skillz is already reporting non-compliance or asserting that Papaya has interposed new privilege objections to compelled materials, that would accelerate the contested discovery timeline and potentially put Papaya before Judge Walrath on a sanctions or further-compel motion before the recognition hearing is even scheduled. That trajectory matters directly to Skillz's ability to build a factual record on its recognition challenges — the same challenges noted in the __[Firy/FIRY Business Wire release carried by Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/israeli-court-says-papaya-gaming-120000588.html)__ as actively contesting recognition "on numerous grounds." The Israeli-side parallel pressure remains: 
Judge Lushi-Abudi rejected Papaya's motion to convene creditors' meetings to vote on its proposed debt settlement, stating that Papaya should strengthen its proposed creditor repayment plan that currently relies only on operating profits, with the risks thereto, without any securities or equity contribution.
 A Papaya that is simultaneously resisting document production in Delaware and unable to satisfy the Israeli court that its repayment plan is adequately secured is a weaker petitioner for recognition on both fronts. The next concrete milestone is the public docketing and, where possible, unsealing of the substance of Dkt. 93, together with Papaya's compliance with whatever production and deposition deadlines Dkt. 92 imposed — those deadlines have not appeared on the public docket and must be confirmed from the order itself.

items.body_md:
On September 2, the Bartz plaintiffs filed a Status Report — Dkt. 688 — disclosing the class distribution mechanics and timeline. 
Class counsel filed the Status Report outlining the distribution plan; per that filing, claimants were to receive a consolidated form listing their works and percentage share of the settlement by September 4.
 
A second payment of approximately $930 per work is projected after Anthropic's next installment of $450 million deposits, due September 25, 2027, bringing the estimated total to just over $3,100 per work — figures the report characterizes as estimates, not guaranteed amounts.
 The Status Report is now the primary reference point for class members and the court on distribution mechanics; its content confirms that the September 25, 2026 first-installment deadline is the operative near-term trigger for the initial payment tranche. No party has moved to modify, stay, or object to the payment schedule as reflected in the filing.

Also on September 3, Kathleen R. Hartnett of Cooley LLP filed a Notice of Withdrawal — Dkt. 689 — terminating her appearance on behalf of Anthropic PBC. Hartnett had been Cooley's lead attorney of record for Anthropic through the pre-settlement litigation phase, including the motion-to-stay briefing in mid-2025. The withdrawal is procedural on its face: the case is post-judgment, both pending Ninth Circuit appeals (No. 26-5391, Edelson PC / Oppenheim + Zebrak; No. 26-5455, Cowan DeBaets Abrahams & Sheppard LLP) are fee-only disputes with no effect on Anthropic's payment obligations, and Douglas Winthrop and other Anthropic counsel remain on the docket. It is worth flagging as context, however, that 
Anthropic appointed a new general counsel in late August 2026, with her predecessor moving into a role coordinating with international governments
 — a corporate-side transition that may account for the rationalization of outside counsel appearances, though no causal link is confirmed on the district docket. The withdrawal has no bearing on the payment schedule or class recovery.

Dkt. 690 — a letter from Karen S. Gordon dated August 20, filed August 20 but docketed September 3 — remains unclassified. The docket supplies no subject matter or relief requested; RECAP has not captured the document. It cannot be characterized without the underlying text and should be pulled directly from PACER. The electronic filing error flagged on September 2 in connection with objector Stacy Lynn Werner's Dkt. 687 remains uncorrected on the visible docket: the clerk directed Werner's counsel to refile using the proper Ninth Circuit Notice of Appeal form, and no conforming notice has appeared. Until a corrected notice is filed and the Ninth Circuit opens a case number for Werner's intervention effort, her appellate posture is in procedural limbo alongside the two fee appeals already docketed as Nos. 26-5391 and 26-5455. Neither of those appeals has drawn a Ninth Circuit scheduling order setting opening-brief deadlines, an open question from prior briefings that remains unresolved. The next concrete milestone is Anthropic's $450 million Scheduled Payment 1, due September 25, 2026; the contents of Dkt. 688 now confirm that first payment is tied directly to that deposit.

items.lede: On September 3, the Poolin docket recorded a Certification of No Objection at Dkt. 200 — procedural in classification and, standing alone, of limited independent weight. The six unidentified documents at Dkts.
items.body_md:
On September 3, the Poolin docket recorded a Certification of No Objection at Dkt. 200 — procedural in classification and, standing alone, of limited independent weight. The six unidentified documents at Dkts. 194–199 (five filed September 2, one filed September 3) remain the outstanding classification problem: public metadata discloses no filer, title, or nature for any of them, and no secondary source has reported on their content. CM/ECF and __[Verita Global](https://veritaglobal.net/poolin)__ are the only routes to retrieve and classify these filings before the September 8 bid deadline four days from now. If any of the six constitutes a qualified bid submission, a sale objection, a motion to adjourn or modify the auction, a supplement to the Rule 9019 compromise at Dkt. 190, or any filing that alters the sale process or its timeline, it is substantive and material — and would require immediate attention from any creditor tracking recovery exposure. The Certification of No Objection at Dkt. 200, absent knowledge of the underlying motion it resolves, cannot be classified with precision; a CNO typically signals an uncontested order about to enter, which could be consequential or routine depending entirely on what motion it closes out.


The next hard dates are September 8 (qualified bid deadline), September 10 (auction, if competing bids are received), and September 16 (sale hearing per Bondoro).
 
A separate source places the sale hearing on September 18 before Judge O'Hagan.
 The September 16 versus September 18 conflict noted in yesterday's briefing remains unresolved in public sources; the operative scheduling order on the docket is the only authoritative reference. 
The auction, if triggered, is scheduled for 10:00 a.m. Eastern, either at the offices of Archer & Greiner in Voorhees, New Jersey, virtually, or at another time and place designated by the debtors.
 
The properties may be sold separately if that structure produces greater value for creditors than transferring the portfolio together; the sale follows a marketing campaign that contacted more than 335 potential purchasers, resulting in 28 confidentiality agreements and seven letters of intent.
 No competing bid above the $52 million stalking-horse floor has been publicly disclosed, and whether any of Dkts. 194–199 changes that picture is the case's central unknown entering the final weekend before the bid deadline.

The Rule 9019 compromise at Dkt. 190 (filed August 28) remains unresolved in public metadata — counterparty, subject matter, and dollar amount are all undisclosed. The trustee motion, with a hearing scheduled for October 21, remains the structural overhang behind the sale: appointment of a Chapter 11 trustee would displace existing management and the CRO, transfer control of the § 363 sale process to a court-appointed fiduciary, and alter who directs distributions to the approximately 11,700 IOU holders. 
Chief Restructuring Officer Michael DuFrayne has placed prepetition obligations at approximately $173.1 million, of which roughly $163.7 million consists of unsecured IOUs issued to Poolin Wallet customers after the company suspended withdrawals during the 2022 market downturn.
 The next concrete milestone is September 8 — the qualified bid deadline, and the first hard data point on whether any bidder is prepared to exceed the stalking-horse floor.

items.body_md:
On September 3, a federal judge in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California ruled that 
Jump Trading LLC and its subsidiaries must face the bulk of a proposed securities class action from investors who claim it misled them and manipulated the market for Terraform Labs' stablecoins in the lead-up to the collapse of the Terraform ecosystem
, per __[Law360](https://www.law360.com/classaction/articles/2521162)__. The ruling is an order surviving a motion to dismiss (or the equivalent threshold challenge); the Law360 report does not specify the precise procedural vehicle denied, and the full order has not been confirmed on the public docket — treat the substance as accurate per a credible outlet but flag that the underlying order itself has not been independently verified. Judge P. Casey Pitts is identified in the Law360 metadata as the presiding judge. This is a separate proceeding from the plan administrator's $4-billion-plus suit against Jump in the Northern District of Illinois; both tracks run in parallel to the Chapter 11 in Bankr. D. Del.

The significance to recovery posture is indirect but meaningful. The investor class action preserves a separate pressure vector on Jump that may accelerate settlement discussions in the plan administrator's suit — Jump now faces coordinated litigation exposure on both the securities-fraud and the contract/unjust-enrichment theories the administrator is pursuing. A settlement in either proceeding that produces cash for the estate would be the most direct near-term recovery catalyst for Class 5 Crypto Loss claimants, whose pool continues to see secondary-market activity: Dkt. 1312 (filed August 3) reflected a $3,454,036.42 Class 5 claim transferred to Serrur Investment Partners, LP, consistent with ongoing claim trading ahead of any distribution.

Dkts. 1329 and 1330, both filed September 3, are listed as "Exhibit" with no further docket description — almost certainly exhibit attachments to a prior substantive filing rather than independent substantive filings, but without full text they cannot be classified up. The authorization motion filed August 19 (Dkt. 1321) still shows no corresponding order on the public record and remains the open near-term item in the bankruptcy itself. The next fixed milestone remains December 31, 2026 — the court-extended wind-down deadline — with resolution of the Jump litigation and *Chang v. Terraform Labs Wind Down Trust* (Adv. Proc. 26-50229) the primary substantive triggers between now and that date.

items.lede: On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here.
items.body_md:
On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here. Given the live motions practice in this case, the most plausible target is Google's August 21 Administrative Motion to Consider Whether Cases Should Be Related (Dkt. 478), whose response deadline was set at August 25 — the same date Dkt. 483 was filed. If that is the motion being opposed, the filing reflects a party — most likely the plaintiff class — resisting Google's effort to link this proceeding to one or more related cases. The case-relation motion, if granted, could shift judicial assignment or coordinate discovery and briefing schedules in ways that affect litigation pace and cost for both sides; if denied, each proceeding continues on its own track. Until Dkt. 483's full text is pulled from PACER, the identity of the filing party, the motion it targets, and the arguments advanced remain unverified and are not stated here.

The more consequential open question from yesterday remains unresolved in any available source: the outcome of the Dkt. 482 omnibus order — which adjudicates class certification, Google's sanctions motion, the outstanding intervention motion (Dkt. 468, Lee Child/Andrew Child/Girlcomix), and three motions for miscellaneous relief — has not been reported by any secondary outlet as of this briefing. The full text of Dkt. 482 on PACER is the controlling document. Until it is pulled, the class's shape, the sanctions disposition, and whether the intervenors were admitted remain unverified. The practical consequence is significant: class certification in this case defines the universe of copyright holders who can share in any statutory-damages recovery, and the per-work structure of § 504(c) means that the breadth of the certified class — authors only, publishers included, works defined by training vs. ingestion — directly sets the ceiling on Google's aggregate exposure.

The next concrete milestone is the resolution of the Dkt. 478 case-relation motion, which is now fully briefed with Dkt. 483's opposition and ripe for ruling. No hearing date is visible in the docket text for that motion. On the merits track, the full text of Dkt. 482 — available on PACER at 5:23-cv-03440 — remains the priority pull; it is the document that determines where this case goes from here.

items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.
